deep.reconstruction:
Setting and purpose (my interpretation, from the formulas). This is an Olbers-type computation for an orbit from two observations, written in a convenient frame. The two geocentric directions of the body lie on a great circle with node N and inclination i. Step 1 defines λ, λ' as the arcs from the node along that circle: tan b = tan i·sin(α−N) and tan λ = tan(α−N)/cos i, and the same with primes. These are the standard spherical relations for a point of longitude α on a great circle of inclination i. With u(λ) the unit vector in that plane, the body's geocentric vectors are ρ·u(λ) and ρ'·u(λ'). The heliocentric chord k between the two positions is |ρu(λ) − ρ'u(λ') − d|. Here d = S − S' is the difference of the Sun's geocentric vectors ("A auf ⊙ Ort sich bezieht": A, A' are the Sun's longitudes, R, R' its distances, B, B' its latitudes, with R tan B as the height).

Step 2: resolve d into the node frame. X = R cos(A−N) − R'cos(A'−N), Y = R sin(A−N) − R' sin(A'−N), Z = R tan B − R' tan B'. Gauss parametrises them as X = p cosψ cos(i−φ), Y = p sinψ cosφ, Z = p sinψ sinφ. Rotating by i about the node line (my step):
- the in-plane components are p cos(i−φ)·(cosψ, sinψ);
- the normal component is ±p sinψ sin(i−φ).

Write q = p cos(i−φ). The in-plane part decomposes obliquely as d∥ = a·u(λ) + b·u(λ'), with a = q sin(λ'−ψ)/sin(λ'−λ) and b = −q sin(λ−ψ)/sin(λ'−λ). Then ρu − ρ'u' − d∥ = x·u − y·u', where x = ρ − a and y = ρ' − q sin(λ−ψ)/sin(λ'−λ). Since |xu − yu'|² = x² + y² − 2xy cos(λ'−λ), this gives Gauss's first expression:
kk = x² + y² − 2·(product)·cos(λ'−λ) + (p sinψ sin(i−φ))².

He then uses x² + y² − 2xy cosΔ = cos²(Δ/2)(x−y)² + sin²(Δ/2)(x+y)², together with sum-to-product formulas (writing Δ = λ'−λ, σ = ½(λ+λ')):
- a − c = q cos(σ−ψ)/cos(Δ/2);
- a + c = q sin(σ−ψ)/sin(Δ/2).
This yields:
kk = cos²(Δ/2){ρ'−ρ + q cos(σ−ψ)/cos(Δ/2)}² + sin²(Δ/2){ρ'+ρ − q sin(σ−ψ)/sin(Δ/2)}² + (p sinψ sin(i−φ))².

Special case with the ecliptic as reference (B = B' = 0, so Z = 0). Now X = D cosψ and Y cos i = D sinψ; the in-plane magnitude is D and the normal component is −D sinψ tan i. Hence:
kk = cos²(Δ/2){ρ'−ρ + D cos(ψ−σ)/cos(Δ/2)}² + sin²(Δ/2){ρ'+ρ + D sin(ψ−σ)/sin(Δ/2)}² + (D sinψ tan i)².

Olbers' substitution ρ' = μρ. Set (1−μ)cos(Δ/2) = t cosθ and (1+μ)sin(Δ/2) = t sinθ. The two brackets, multiplied out, become −tρ cosθ + D cos(ψ−σ) and tρ sinθ + D sin(ψ−σ). Their squares sum to t²ρ² − 2tρD cos(θ+ψ−σ) + D², which equals (tρ − D cos(θ+ψ−σ))² + D² sin²(θ+ψ−σ). With et = −D cos(θ+ψ−σ) and f = D·√(sin²(θ+ψ−σ) + sin²ψ tan²i), this gives kk = tt(ρ+e)² + ff.

Thus the chord is reduced to a sum of two squares in the single unknown ρ, ready for iteration with Euler's/Lambert's equation. The right-margin column (0.000 → 0.3010…, increasing about 0.0005 per step) is the start of a table continued on the next page. Its function is unidentified; log10 2 = 0.30103 is the value at 0. It appears unrelated to the derivation.
errors: Line 1 of kk: the last term is written '(p sinψ sin i−φ)²'. Parentheses are missing; it should be (p sinψ sin(i−φ))², as Gauss writes correctly two lines later.
The first sum-of-squares form has (ρ'−ρ) in the first brace. This is the negative of x−y, which is harmless because the brace is squared.

The definition of f: if the symbol before the parenthesis were read as D·D (i.e. f = D²(…)), the final kk = tt(ρ+e)² + ff would be wrong. The consistent reading is f = D·√(sin²(θ+ψ−σ) + sin²ψ tan²i), i.e. the mark is a radical sign. Otherwise all steps check out (the sign of the normal component is irrelevant since it is squared).
The crossed-out 'ttϱ+e' is a corrected slip, replaced by tt(ϱ+e)²+ff.

results.what: Reduction of geocentric positions to arcs λ, λ' on a great circle (node N, inclination i): tan b = tan i sin(α−N), tan λ = tan(α−N)/cos i
results.modern_name: Right-angled spherical triangle relations / coordinate rotation to the orbit or great-circle frame
results.usually_credited_to: classical (Napier's rules; Euler and Lagrange era)

results.what: Chord k² between two positions as quadratic in the geocentric distances, using oblique decomposition and the half-angle sum-of-squares identity x²+y²−2xy cosΔ = cos²(Δ/2)(x−y)² + sin²(Δ/2)(x+y)²
results.modern_name: Chord computation in Olbers' method for parabolic orbits
results.usually_credited_to: W. Olbers (1797); Gauss refined such reductions (Theoria Motus, 1809)

results.what: With ρ' = μρ, auxiliary angles t, θ, e, f give kk = t²(ρ+e)² + f²
results.modern_name: Auxiliary-angle (Gaussian) reduction of a quadratic to a sum of squares for logarithmic computation; Olbers' M-ratio

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard working-out of the chord formula in Olbers' method, using Gauss's well-known auxiliary-angle style. It is fully consistent with his published orbit-determination work of 1805–1809, and nothing here is new.

transcription_corrections: The symbol in 'D (sin(θ+ψ−½λ−½λ')² + sinψ² tang i²) = f' appears to be a radical sign: D√(…) = f. This is consistent with kk = tt(ϱ+e)² + ff.
In the first sum-of-squares form, the first brace is 'ϱ' − ϱ' with an overwritten sign; the second term is 'sin(½λ+½λ'−ψ)'.
